messages:
anna: Heads up — noticed a CPU-side perf regression on the scheduler path after the batching refactor merged to main. Flamegraph from perf shows Python frames (scheduler/batching) dominating; end-to-end latency up ~18% on p3.xlarge benchmark.

josh: Ugh. Which run did you profile? nsys or perf?

anna: perf (system-wide, -F 99 -g) on the worker hosting the batching hot loop. Also did a short py-spy sampling to sanity-check. nsys run exists too but that's for GPU kernels — here the CPU is the bottleneck pre/post kernel dispatch.

priya: Do you have the folded stacks or flame svg?

anna: Put commands and outputs below. Flame attached (internal link): s3://redwood-perf/runs/1789/anna-flame.svg
```bash
# repro steps
perf record -F 99 -g -- python3 bench_infer.py --model gpt-small --batch 8 --seq 1024
perf script > out.perf
./FlameGraph/stackcollapse-perf.pl out.perf > out.folded
./FlameGraph/flamegraph.pl out.folded > flame.svg
```

anna: Key hotspots from the top of the flame (rough sample % over 60s):
- python scheduler.py:allocate_tokens_and_route ~38%
- batching.py:merge_requests ~20%
- tokenizer/fast.py:tokenize_batch ~12%
- libc/memmove and memcpy ~15% (mostly in data marshalling)
- syscall time very low (io not the issue)

liam: 38% on scheduler sounds like we're spending Python CPU in the hot path. Is that the new batching policy doing heavy Python work per token?

anna: Yes — after the refactor we added per-request heuristics (priority checks + KV cache lookup) inside the main loop in Python. Previously some of that logic was pushed down into C++ glue.

josh: Can you paste the minimal stack sample (collapsed) for the scheduler frames?

anna: Sure — example collapsed line from out.folded:
```
python3;python;PyEval_EvalFrameEx;redwood.runtime.scheduler.process_batch;redwood.runtime.scheduler._route_and_merge;redwood.runtime.batching.merge_requests
```

priya: That points at pure Python call overhead and frame traversal. Two options: move hot inner loop to C extension/Cython, or reduce per-request callbacks (vectorize heuristics).

liam: Before we jump to C, can we try improving sampling fidelity: run perf with --call-graph dwarf and build Python with frame pointers? Also try py-spy (native) to confirm. Sometimes perf overcounts because of interpreter frames.

anna: I ran with dwarf too. py-spy confirmed similar distribution (py-spy top shows scheduler.* at ~35-40%).

perf-bot: nsys capture completed: /nsys/runs/1789/1789-nsys-capture.qdrep (size 2.9GB) — GPU kernels normal, no kernel-time regression.

josh: Good — means kernel selection path likely unchanged. It's the pre-kernel orchestration on CPU.

priya: What's the KV cache hit cost? Are we doing expensive Python-level dict lookups per token?

anna: KV cache lookup is currently in Python because we need to check tag metadata; result shows ~8% of total CPU is spent in kv_cache.get() (pure Python). We could tag cache entries with a shallow C struct and do mmap-friendly lookups, but that's a bigger change.

liam: Quick mitigation: short-circuit common case. If request->cacheable flag is set, skip metadata checks. Can we add a fast-path boolean that is computed once when request is enqueued?

anna: I prototyped that locally — reduced scheduler time from 38% to ~28% in a short run. Still heavy, but promising.

josh: Nice. Also consider batching the tokenization calls: right now tokenize_batch is called per merged request; maybe merge input byte buffers earlier and call tokenizer in C extension once for the combined buffer, then split results. That will move memmove cost into tokenizer C code and reduce Python overhead.

priya: Agreed. Another experiment: run bench with pypy or enable PGO for CPython — sometimes interpreter overhead drops. But C path will still win.

anna: I've queued a follow-up perf run with these experiments: (1) fast-path flag, (2) merged-tokenize prototype, (3) Cython-ized inner loop (micro change). Will attach diff.

anna: Short diff for scheduler micro-change:
```diff
--- a/redwood/runtime/scheduler.py
+++ b/redwood/runtime/scheduler.py
@@
-    for req in pending:
-        if should_check_metadata(req):
-            do_metadata_check(req)
+    pending_list = list(pending)  # avoid mutation and reduce iterator overhead
+    for req in pending_list:
+        # fast-path: single boolean check avoids heavy metadata inspection
+        if not req._cache_check_needed:
+            route_quick(req)
+            continue
+        if should_check_metadata(req):
+            do_metadata_check(req)
```

liam: That looks fine as a short-term perf tweak. But note that list(pending) allocates; measure allocation cost. If the hot path runs often, allocation may regress. Try using itertools.islice or prealloc small array in C.

anna: Good point — allocation accounted for ~2% in flame (object allocs). I kept an eye on it but will benchmark both ways.

josh: For the longer-term fix, consider moving the whole routing merge into a C++ RT (native module) that exposes a single call merge_and_route(pending_list) -> merged_batches. Then do minimal Python per-batch. That matches our prior architecture for GPU dispatch.

priya: Yes. Also add perf regression tests into CI: run a short perf trace on microbench and fail if scheduler p99 or flame sample share exceeds threshold. We can automate with perf script -> stackcollapse -> compare top n stacks.

anna: I'm working on that; prototype script compares folded output and checks relative share for scheduler.* frames. If > 25% and changed by > +5% we flag.

liam: One more measurement idea: run perf with user-level cmap for sample attribution across threads so we can separate worker thread scheduler vs main process. Also run with perf --kcore to catch kernel+libc hotspots.

anna: Next steps (tracked):
- finish merged-tokenize experiment and run perf/py-spy (assigned: anna)
- prototype C-extension for inner loop (assigned: josh/priya)
- add CI perf-smoke check for scheduler frames (assigned: priya)
- iterate on fast-path flag to avoid per-request metadata checks (assigned: anna)

josh: Thanks — please paste final flame svg and the small perf script in the thread when done. Keep GPU traces too — good to have full context.

anna: Will do. If anyone wants to pair on the C-extension I'll ping. :coffee: 

perf-bot: scheduled perf-smoke job #5789 — will run on ci-perf01 in ~10m and post results.

liam: Quick note — when converting to C ext, prefer a minimal API (bytes in, list of offsets out) and avoid GIL for the hot loop.

anna: Yup — we discussed releasing GIL around the merge logic. Alright folks, rerun in ~1hr with the fast-path flag results, will update here.

josh: Thanks — nice triage. :thumbsup:
